The final output stage applied to every audio path. Controls global volume, stereo balance, and a hard ceiling that prevents clipping.

• **Output Gain** — raises or lowers overall loudness. Increase for louder output; decrease if the signal clips downstream.
• **Output Pan** — shifts the stereo image left or right. Center (0) is neutral; positive values push the image right.
• **Threshold Limit** — sets the hard-limiter ceiling in dB. Lower values catch louder peaks earlier, preventing distortion at the cost of some dynamic range.

Automatic Gain Control (AGC) that continuously measures the output level and adjusts gain to keep perceived loudness consistent across tracks with different recorded volumes.

• **Strength** — how aggressively the AGC reacts to level changes. Higher values produce faster, tighter leveling; lower values allow more natural dynamics.
• **Max Gain** — caps the maximum amplification the AGC can apply. Prevents over-boosting quiet content to the point of noise amplification.
• **Output Threshold** — the target ceiling level in dB. The AGC tries to keep the output at or below this level; lower values leave more headroom.

Measures integrated loudness (LUFS) in real time and applies a gain offset to bring the signal to a target loudness level. Useful for normalizing music to streaming standards (e.g. -14 LUFS).

• **Target LUFS** — the desired integrated loudness. Lower (more negative) values produce a quieter, more dynamic result; higher values bring everything up to a louder reference.
• **Max Gain** — limits how much boost can be applied. Prevents extremely quiet passages from being over-amplified.
• **Speed** — how quickly the gain adjusts. Slow tracks broad program changes; Fast reacts to moment-to-moment level shifts, which can sound more aggressive.

A professional FET-style dynamics compressor modeled on classic hardware like the UREI 1176. Reduces dynamic range by attenuating loud peaks, adding punch and density to the signal.

• **Threshold** — the level where compression begins. Lower values start compressing earlier, affecting more of the signal.
• **Ratio** — compression intensity. Higher ratio = more squashed dynamics. 1.0 = no compression.
• **Knee / Auto Knee** — transition smoothness at the threshold. Higher knee values create a softer, more transparent onset.
• **Gain / Auto Gain** — make-up gain after compression. Restores perceived loudness lost during gain reduction.
• **Attack** — how quickly compression engages. Fast attack catches transients; slow attack lets them through for a punchier sound.
• **Release** — how quickly compression disengages. Fast release can cause pumping; slow release sounds more natural.
• **Crest** — the level-detection window in ms. Short windows (5-20 ms) react to sharp transient peaks; longer windows (100-300 ms) average the program level, producing smoother, less pumping compression.
• **Adapt** — enables program-adaptive timing. Higher values let the compressor adjust behavior to the audio material.
• **No Clip** — hard-limits output to 0 dBFS, preventing any digital clipping after compression.

A 5-band compressor splitting audio into Sub, Low, Mid, Presence, and Air bands compressed independently. Allows targeted dynamics control without one band affecting another.

• **Band Enabled** — activates or bypasses compression for the selected band.
• **Upper Crossover** — the frequency at which this band hands off to the next. Reshapes which frequencies each band controls.
• **Threshold** — compression onset level for this band. Lower values affect more of the signal.
• **Ratio** — compression intensity per band. Higher = more dynamic reduction in this frequency range.
• **Knee / Auto Knee** — transition smoothness for this band.
• **Gain / Auto Gain** — make-up gain for this band. Restores body or air lost during compression.
• **Attack / Max Attack** — transient response. Fast on Sub tightens bass punch; slow on Mid preserves vocal presence.
• **Release / Max Release** — recovery speed. Affects how naturally each band breathes.
• **Crest** — peak vs. RMS sensing for this band.
• **Adapt** — program-adaptive timing for this band.
• **No Clip** — prevents this band's output from exceeding 0 dBFS.

ViPER Device Dependent Correction. Loads a .vdc impulse profile that applies a frequency-response correction curve measured for a specific headphone or earphone model, compensating for its acoustic deviations and targeting a neutral or Harman-style response.\n\n\u2022 **Headset Correction** \u2014 selects the .vdc file for your headphone or earphone model. Choosing the correct profile produces the most accurate, balanced tonality. Selecting None disables the correction.

Reconstructs high-frequency content lost or rolled off during recording, encoding, or compression (e.g. MP3 artifacts). Uses harmonic synthesis to generate plausible high-frequency energy.

• **Strength** — upper frequency limit of harmonic synthesis (2.2-8.2 kHz). Lower values add warmth and air in the upper midrange; higher values extend presence further into the treble.
• **Exciter** — blends in additional harmonic brightness on top of the reconstructed spectrum. Higher values add perceived detail and sparkle, but too much can sound harsh or artificial.

A FIR (Finite Impulse Response) linear-phase equalizer. Unlike IIR filters, FIR introduces zero phase distortion, preserving stereo imaging and transient accuracy at the cost of added latency.

• **Band Count** — selects 10, 15, 25, or 31 bands. More bands allow finer tonal shaping and narrower per-band control.
• **Band Sliders** — each band boosts or cuts a fixed frequency. Boost to add presence; cut to reduce harshness or muddiness.
• **Preset** — applies a predefined curve (e.g. Bass Booster, Acoustic) as a starting point.
• **Custom Preset** — saves and recalls your own EQ curves across sessions.

A per-band equalizer where each band only applies gain when the input at that frequency exceeds a threshold. Acts like a frequency-selective compressor rather than a static tonal adjustment.

• **Frequency** — center frequency of the band. Set to the frequency you want to control dynamically (e.g. 6-8 kHz for de-essing sibilance).
• **Q Factor** — bandwidth. Higher Q = narrower, more surgical; lower Q = broader and more musical.
• **Filter Type** — shape of the band: Peak applies a symmetric bell boost/cut around the center frequency; Low Shelf affects everything below it; High Shelf affects everything above. This fundamentally changes which part of the spectrum is dynamically controlled.
• **Target Gain** — gain applied when the threshold is exceeded. Negative = dynamic cut; positive = dynamic boost.
• **Threshold** — signal level that triggers the band. Only signals above this are affected.
• **Attack** — how fast the band engages when the threshold is exceeded.
• **Release** — how fast the band returns to neutral after the signal drops below the threshold.

Applies convolution processing using an impulse response (IR) file. The IR encodes the acoustic signature of a real space or device; convolving the audio with it imprints that signature onto the signal.

• **Kernel File** — the .wav impulse response to load. A room IR adds natural reverberation; a speaker/headphone IR corrects or transforms the frequency response to match that device's sound.
• **Cross-Channel** — blends left-channel IR into the right and vice versa. Higher values increase stereo width and diffusion by mixing the stereo impulse responses.

Widens and deepens the stereo field by processing the mid and side components, creating a more enveloping sense of space without headphone-specific HRTFs.

• **Surround Strength** — how far the soundstage extends. Higher values create a wider, more immersive image but can make the center sound distant.
• **Mid Image Strength** — prominence of the center image (vocals, lead instruments). Higher values push the center forward and more defined.
• **Depth** — front-to-back dimension. Higher values make some elements sound farther away, increasing perceived three-dimensionality.

Extracts the difference (side) signal and delays it relative to the mid signal to create a diffuse, enveloping surround effect from standard stereo content.

• **Delay** — time offset applied to the side signal in ms. Larger delays produce a more spacious, hall-like surround effect.
• **Reverse** — inverts polarity of the side signal. Creates an alternative spatial character; useful when the default delay causes phase issues.
• **Wet/Dry Mix** — balances the processed surround signal with the original. Lower values give a subtle enhancement; higher values produce a strong immersive effect.
• **LP Cutoff** — low-pass filter on the side signal (0 = disabled). When set above 0, frequencies above the cutoff are rolled off from the surround effect, keeping the diffuse sound natural and preventing a harsh, airy treble spread.

A 3-band stereo width processor controlling the width of low, mid, and high frequency ranges independently, allowing precise stereo field shaping.

• **Low Width** — width of the bass band. Below 100% narrows bass toward mono (tighter, better mono compatibility); above 100% widens the low end.
• **Mid Width** — width of the midrange. Narrowing focuses the midrange; widening pushes instruments farther apart.
• **High Width** — width of the high-frequency band. Widening adds air and spaciousness; narrowing reduces listener fatigue.
• **Low Crossover** — frequency boundary between Low and Mid bands.
• **High Crossover** — frequency boundary between Mid and High bands.

Headphone Surround+ (VHE) applies Head-Related Transfer Function (HRTF) processing to simulate loudspeakers in a room through headphones, reducing the unnatural in-head localization typical of headphone listening.\n\n\u2022 **Quality Level (0-4)** \u2014 selects the HRTF algorithm complexity. Level 0 is the lightest and most subtle; Level 4 uses the most sophisticated HRTF set for the most convincing speaker-in-room simulation, but uses more CPU. Levels 2-3 offer a balanced result for most listeners.

Adds algorithmic reverberation to simulate acoustic spaces, from a small room to a large concert hall.

• **Room Size** — perceived size of the simulated space. Larger values produce longer, more spacious reverb tails.
• **Width** — stereo spread of the reverb tail. Higher values create a wider, more enveloping reverb; lower values keep it centered.
• **Dampening** — high-frequency absorption in the simulated space. Higher values produce a warmer, darker tail (like soft furnishings); lower values simulate hard, reflective surfaces.
• **Wet Signal** — level of the processed reverb signal. Increase for more reverb presence.
• **Dry Signal** — level of the unprocessed original signal. Reduce for a fully wet, ambient effect.

A dynamic bass enhancement engine using an X/Y frequency curve to add low-frequency weight and impact, optimized for headphones and earphones.

• **Dynamic Bass Strength** — overall intensity of the bass enhancement. Higher values produce a stronger, more prominent bass boost.
• **X Low / X High Freq** — define the frequency range of the primary bass boost curve. Lowering X Low extends boost deeper into sub-bass; raising X High brings it further into the midbass.
• **Y Low / Y High Freq** — control the gain contour within the X frequency range, shaping how the enhancement rises and falls across the bass spectrum.
• **Side Gain Low / High** — adjust the stereo side channel level in the low and high portions of the bass band. Modifies whether enhanced bass feels wide or tight and mono.
• **Device Preset** — loads an optimized curve for a headphone category (e.g. Extreme Headphone v2). A quick starting point before fine-tuning.

Generates perceived bass by synthesizing harmonics of the fundamental frequency. The auditory system reconstructs a missing fundamental from its harmonics, allowing bass to be felt even on small speakers or earphones that cannot reproduce deep sub-bass directly.

• **Cutoff** — upper frequency limit of the bass band processed for harmonic generation. Lower values (60 Hz) focus on deep sub-bass; higher values (150 Hz) extend into upper bass.
• **Intensity** — strength of the synthesized harmonics. Higher values make the effect more powerful but too much can introduce a buzzy, artificial quality.
• **Harmonic Order** — which harmonic of the fundamental is synthesized (2nd-5th). Lower orders (2nd, 3rd) sound warmer and more musical; higher orders (4th, 5th) sound brighter and more aggressive.
• **Original Bass Level** — mix level of the original bass signal. Lowering it reduces boom while keeping perceived bass through the psychoacoustic effect.

A multi-mode bass enhancement that increases low-frequency weight and impact, with three different processing characters.

• **Mode** — selects the algorithm: Natural Bass applies a smooth low-shelf boost with minimal coloration; Pure Bass+ uses nonlinear saturation for a more powerful, textured result; Subwoofer restricts and maximizes bass energy below the selected frequency for deep, sub-like impact.
• **Frequency** — crossover/cutoff frequency. Lower values (15-40 Hz) target deep sub-bass only; higher values (up to 150 Hz) extend the enhancement into the midbass for more warmth and body.
• **Gain** — amount of bass boost. Higher values produce louder, more prominent bass but can cause distortion if excessive.
• **Fade-in** — prevents a loud click transient when the effect is enabled mid-playback by slowly ramping gain up.

Identical to ViPER Bass but additionally sums the bass frequency band to mono before processing. Eliminates phase cancellation artifacts common in stereo bass content, producing a tighter, more focused low end especially beneficial for headphone listening.

• **Mode** — Natural Bass, Pure Bass+, or Subwoofer (same as ViPER Bass).
• **Frequency** — content below this point is summed to mono and enhanced.
• **Gain** — bass boost level.
• **Fade-in** — ramps gain on enable to avoid transient clicks.

Enhances high-frequency detail, presence, and perceived resolution through three distinct processing modes.

• **Mode** — selects the algorithm: Natural applies a gentle high-shelf lift for added air; OZone+ uses psychoacoustic harmonic excitation to add perceived resolution and openness without a simple treble boost; XHiFi applies a more aggressive enhancement targeting a hi-fi, detail-forward character.
• **Gain** — intensity of the selected mode. Higher values make the effect more pronounced and noticeable.

Auditory System Protection. Applies binaural crossfeed that simulates the natural inter-aural crosstalk of loudspeaker listening, reducing headphone fatigue over long listening sessions.\n\n\u2022 **Binaural Level** \u2014 selects crossfeed intensity: Off disables the effect; Mild applies gentle blending that subtly reduces stereo separation; Medium offers balanced crossfeed similar to moderate speaker listening; Strong applies heavy crossfeed for a very speaker-like, centered image that minimizes in-head localization.

Simulates the harmonic saturation and coloration of a 6N1J dual-triode vacuum tube preamplifier stage. Adds subtle even-order harmonic distortion that imparts warmth, smoothness, and an analog character.\n\nThere are no adjustable parameters. Toggle on for a warmer, more vintage-sounding output; toggle off to restore a clean, uncolored signal.

Simulates the nonlinear behavior and harmonic distortion of analog audio circuit topologies including amplifier stages, transformers, and tape.\n\n\u2022 **Mode** \u2014 selects the circuit model and intensity: Mild applies the subtlest coloration for barely-there warmth; Medium adds more harmonic richness and body; Strong applies heavier saturation with a pronounced vintage analog character. Higher modes add more perceived density and loudness alongside the coloration.

Applies a digital correction filter optimized for the device\'s built-in speakers, compensating for their measured frequency response and phase deviations to produce a flatter, more accurate sound.\n\nThere are no adjustable parameters. Enable when listening through the built-in speakers for more balanced tonality; disable when using headphones or external speakers.
